en: [Pūrvapakṣa:

Just as there is no distinction whatsoever between existent and non-existent things in their own nature, it is certain that such a distinction likewise does not exist between the insentient and the sentient. (UtAjP 01)

Vṛ: In the view of those who maintain the doctrine of the continuum of consciousness (*vijñānasantāna*), because all entities are momentary, there is no distinction within their own individual, particular natures consisting of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), since a single unifying subject belonging to the continuum is not admitted;
thus, even for sentient and insentient things, there is a lack of distinction within themselves.
Manifestation, description, and existence—whatever constitutes non-existence is their opposite;
this does not touch the intrinsic nature of the thing, for that [nature] resides within the knower. (UtAjP 02)

Vṛtti: Even though one intends to establish the existence or non-existence of entities through manifestation (*prakhyā*) and description (*upākhyā*), characterized respectively by luminosity (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), as well as by their absence, there is nonetheless no contact with the true nature (*svarūpa*) of the object;
for since that manifestation and so forth are attributes of the knower, there is consequently no establishment of the object's own nature.

It is also not tenable that the nature of an object consists in its being the domain of cognition and verbal designation; for if it were to lack a single form due to its dependence on something else, it would overstep its very existence as a real entity.

Vṛtti: Furthermore, even if it were the object of manifestation and so forth, the nature of a category (padārtha) would not be established, because that [manifestation] depends upon being illuminated by another.
Moreover, even if there were multiple forms, the existence of the entity itself would remain unestablished.
Therefore, there is no distinction between the entity and its absence.
Let there be no distinction [between them] based on the presence or absence of manifestation and so forth;
nevertheless, a distinction is indeed established here by that much alone, and that is sufficient for our purpose.

Vṛ: Even if one accepts that there is no distinction [between the two], the existence and non-existence of the two entities—being and non-being—are indeed complete in their manifestation and so forth; since, by relying on those, the possession of specific qualities is once again established, then the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) among all things would necessarily be established in its entirety.
Even so, there would be an adherence to appearances consistent with the nature of sentient beings;
for without depending on that [appearance], there would be no distinction between existence and non-existence.
Vṛtti: And thus, the propriety of the existence of an object—characterized by its being manifest—is conceived as being necessarily bound up with manifestation;

otherwise, in the absence of connection with consciousness, because the existent and non-existent are mutually independent, no distinction could arise between two things each abiding in its own nature.
How could there be no distinction here, since that which is real performs a causal function, while the other does not? Even so, the object remains indistinguishable within its own nature.

Vṛ: [Objection: Since causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) belongs only to an existing entity and its absence belongs to a non-existent one, how can there be no distinction? For it is precisely by means of causal efficiency that the existence of that [entity] is established. To this, he replies: Even so, because causal efficiency depends upon this or that specific cognizer and thus lacks inherent nature (*naisargikatva*), an object cannot be proven to impart a specific quality to itself without relying upon consciousness (*saṃvit*).
Thus, an object that has come to be differentiated by the adjuncts appearing as causal efficiency would exist by its own nature; however, that which is non-existent is not distinguished [from it].

Vṛ: Since consciousness is non-abiding in the manner described, even if an object—which is differentiated by various limiting adjuncts consisting of appearances that perform causal functions—possesses existence in its own objective form, a distinction from a non-existent object would still not be established.
Even there, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) has not been described as establishing the existence of an object;
therefore, the establishment of both [perception and inference] equally depends upon consciousness.

Vṛ: Since causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not established even in the case of an object that is neither existent nor non-existent because it is not yet proven, whereas it is established in the case of an object already proven, causal efficiency itself is not the essence of a real entity (*vastu*).

Therefore, the establishment of both existence and non-existence occurs simultaneously and depends solely upon consciousness, precisely because the determinations of existence are grounded in that [consciousness].

If even consciousness were of a nature devoid of self-reflection, then it too, like the previously mentioned insentient non-existence, would be identical to the Self [in its lack of subjectivity]. (UtAjP 09)

Vṛtti: Even for a light devoid of self-reflective awareness (*nirvimarśa*), although it may manifest the universe like a crystal and so forth, because it lacks autonomy, its similarity would consist only in being an insentient entity that does not exist within itself; by this, the refutation of the doctrine of a quiescent Brahman (*śāntabrahmavāda*) is indicated through the implication of mutual lack of knowledge regarding their respective functions.
Since that very [nature] has not attained final establishment even by its own self-existent essence, how could it become the locus of support for another entity? (UtAjP 10)

Vṛtti: Consciousness that is devoid of self-reflection does not possess its own existence inherently; it is therefore incapable of establishing another, just as a sky-flower is incapable of producing fragrance and the like.
This [object], once it has become established in the light of consciousness as "this," then proceeds again toward the state of being the self through the [egoic] "I. (UtAjP 11)

Vṛtti: An object that has become differentiated is fit for manifestation through the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*); it must then again attain its established state as the nature of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*).

Consciousness alone, consisting of the vibration of the universe, throbbing by its own sovereignty as a non-differentiated manifestation whose essence is the nature of diverse objects, is the life-force of the world.
Without resting in that "I-ness," how could that which is not established in itself be fit for worldly transaction?
For the determination of the other [the insentient] through both positive and negative concomitance is called its establishment, its foundation, its proof, and its accomplishment. (UtAjp 12)
Vṛtti: When established in the knower, it exists; otherwise, it does not exist.

Since its own nature consists in the absence of dependence on another, self-luminosity exists when that [dependence] is absent and does not exist when it is present; thus, the determination of its own-nature versus other-nature is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
And this is expressed by such terms as "establishment" (vyavasthā) and "foundation" (pratiṣṭhā).
Thus, these insentient things exist only as false conceptualizations within the self;
it is light alone that exists, by its own nature and by the natures of both itself and others.

Commentary (Vṛ): Thus, because insentient entities are like non-existence without resting in consciousness, they lack an intrinsic nature in themselves; their existence is solely by virtue of being related to the Knower, whose nature is light.

Therefore, the Teacher has indicated the unfolding of the doctrine of Absolute Freedom (svātantryavāda): that the very light of consciousness, through its own self-surging, [manifests] the manifold variety of the universe brought forth by its own power of Māyā as two masses of entities—sentient and insentient, consisting of the knower and the known—which, though not distinct from its own essence, appear as if they were distinct.

Nor indeed does there exist even an experience that determines [an object] as either different or non-different, apart from a manifestation of continuity whose nature is devoid of reflective awareness (vimarśa). (UtAjP 14)

Vṛtti: Apart from sovereignty, which consists in the unification and disunification [of all things], there can be no experience characterized by creative effort (*saṃrambha*) for an existent that is a mere inert manifestation, because it lacks the nature of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

This indeed is the majesty of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*): that it causes the universe, which resides within as one with its own self, to appear externally as "this," and yet, even while appearing as such, brings it back to non-difference through repose in the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*).
The fulfillment of this reflective awareness of "this," which was previously fragmented, is that repose in one's own essential nature; that reflective awareness is precisely "I am. (UtAjP 15)

Vṛtti: That state of fulfillment characterized by the repose within the very nature of consciousness—which belongs to this insentient object that is perceived as "this" through its distinctness—is precisely this "I" who shines forth as the diverse variety of those various entities. Because of the identity with the light of consciousness, it consists of the reflective awareness of "I," and serves as the very life-force [of all things].

When even an insentient object, through its identity with the cognizing subject whose nature is that of a reflector, attains sentience by resting in the state of "I-ness," and since those sentient things are in reality of the same single nature as the supreme subject— this is the essential meaning: the non-dual state of the sentient subject alone unfolds in its complete fullness everywhere.
This very Self is twofold: the limited and likewise the unlimited;
the former is minute, being constricted by the vital breaths and so forth, while the Supreme Self is indivisible.

Vṛtti: That very Supreme Lord, whose nature is consciousness, through His own will, desiring to manifest the play of the universe, manifests Himself as the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth; having become contracted by assuming the state of being that subject, He attains the condition of a living soul (*jīva*).

However, when the vital breath and other factors are not restricted, He remains the full, independent conscious Self (*cidātman*) due to His nature of overflowing with the entire universe. Thus, there is a twofold state according to whether He is limited or unlimited.
This is the ultimate ground for the cognition of all objects for both [the subject and the object];
because they are linked as one, no other [ground] is possible.

Vṛtti: This twofold [subject], whose nature is light, serves as the locus of rest for all cognitions of objects, whether they consist of existence or non-existence. And since it is of a single form consisting solely in the radiance of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) by virtue of being the synthesizer of what precedes and follows, differentiation is untenable.
Furthermore, in the "I-consciousness," whose nature is the self-reflection of non-differentiation,
no insentient object appears as something additional to its own manifestation, even when it exists at the periphery.

Vṛtti: Furthermore, within the light of the "I" (*ahaṃprakāśa*), which is the nature of the reflective awareness non-different from the universe and the ground of rest for all cognitions, there is no existence for the insentient by virtue of any excess in its own manifestation;
for that [insentient] is undermined by the conceptual alternatives of difference and non-difference from the light of consciousness.

Therefore, the meaning is this: the one non-insentient subject alone, through his own sovereignty, shines forth while manifesting and dissolving the multitude of objects—which are non-different from himself—within his very self, without ever falling away from the stability of his own nature.
Even though it is inherent in cognition and so forth, it is not established merely by its non-manifestation;
therefore, that [self] which possesses breath and so forth would be an object of knowledge, and not the knower, because of the resulting error. (UtAjP 19)

Vṛtti: Although the limited cognizer (*parimitapramātṛ*) is endowed with qualities such as knowledge, he does not achieve [the status of a true subject] precisely due to the absence of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), because if there were a lack of *vimarśa*, the consequence would be insentience (*jāḍya*).

Therefore, by resorting to the delusion of being delimited, the state of being an object of cognition belongs to the one who is the subject consisting of the vital breath and the *puryaṣṭaka*; the status of being the ultimate cognizer (*paramārthapramātṛ*) is not possible [for him].
Even though the stability of objects is restricted within the individual soul (jīva), which is constrained by the vital breaths and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka),
it nevertheless remains established in the Supreme Self (paramātman).

Vṛtti: Although in the worldly course, which consists of the empirical transaction of *māyā*, the arrangement of all external and internal objects is regulated within the individual soul (*jīva*)— which possesses contraction such as vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth— nevertheless, that [arrangement] abides precisely in the nature of Śiva, who is the Supreme Subject, by means of casting off contraction within that limited subject whose self is contracted, because the vital breath and so forth are non-different from the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*).
This is because the state of being an individual soul (aṇu) is accepted through the assumption of the condition of a bound creature (paśubhūmikā), which has been manifested by Śiva’s own will.
How could there be for him any restraint by means of the vital breath, since it has been established in the *Pratyabhijñā* that his very self is the supreme life-force of non-apprehension? (UtAjP 21)

Vṛ: Therefore, how could there be a cessation of the manifestation of Śiva—who is in reality non-different from the nature of Śiva and consists of the flashing forth of the full *ahaṃ* (I-consciousness) composed of unconditioned light and bliss—by means of a limited subject such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) or the like, which is like a fragment of mother-of-pearl?
For if that were the case, it would be impossible for Him to remain as He is; rather, there is simply a failure to manifest the expansion of His own unlimited power.
Thus, the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) is a synonym for the state of being a bound subject;
and since this has been determined in detail in the scripture *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, it should be investigated from that very source.
There is no establishment of objects in the vital breath and so forth, because the sense of "I" has ceased;
for the sense of "I" is proclaimed to be the resting of light within itself. (UtAjP 22)
That very state is called rest, because of the cessation of all dependence;
it is also autonomy, primary agency, and even lordship. (UtAjP 23)

Vṛtti: In the case of insentient things such as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which serve as the locus for limited subjects, there is no establishment of reality whatsoever because of the obstruction of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), which consists in the flashing forth of one's own self alone; for that [establishment of reality] is grounded in consciousness.

Since that very resting of consciousness within its own self is celebrated as the state of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*)—whose nature is the reflective awareness of the full "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*)—it is that which establishes objects.
That itself is the "resting place," because it is the ultimate ground of support for all phenomenal entities.
In its universal expansion, because it is independent of any causal complex external to itself, there is autonomy;
that very autonomy is proclaimed in the scriptures as primary agency and sovereignty.
Māyā is indeed that very power, since no other is established;
for the Lord, as the creator of this world, consists of the non-manifestation of that [power]. (UtAjP 24)
Commentary (Vṛ): Māyā is the power of Śiva, which is non-different from the possessor of power; it consists in the concealment of one's own nature and is his sport.

It is precisely because of this [power] that this universe, consisting of non-recognition (akhyāti), appears, for no other cause is established, as it is undermined by the conceptual dilemmas of difference and non-difference.
Therefore, the state of being the creator of the manifestations of the universe is sovereignty (īśvaratva).
And through its continuous connection, that single [consciousness] is said to be the essence of all cognitions;
it is the reality of the subject, synonymous with self-awareness, and is beginningless. (UtAjP 25)

Vṛtti: That sovereign supreme power (*parā-śakti*), by relying on the unification of all discrete cognitions—such as blue or sword—within their respective functions of joining and separating, or within the limits of "prior" and "subsequent," is one and the same as that which delimits those [cognitions] which constitute its support;
that very thing is called the beginningless reality (*tattva*) of the subject (*mātṛ*), synonymous with self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
The persistence of existence is the culmination for that which partakes in the sense of "I";
its pervasiveness consists in continuity, which is not possible for that which is insentient.

Commentary (Vṛ): Since the non-inert subject—the self of consciousness whose essence is the reflective awareness of the full "I-ness" (pūrṇāhaṃtā)—is inseparable from freedom (svātantrya), it possesses pervasiveness (vyāpitva) consisting of a continuous synthesis (anusaṃdhāna) throughout all things, wherein the establishment of all objects is grounded.
This [pervasiveness] is not possible for an inert thing that lacks freedom, because it lacks the essence of reflective awareness (vimarśa).
Therefore, it is only when there is a distinction within manifestation that the state of being manifested is possible;
for this reason, it was stated in the *Pratyabhijñā* that "this world consists of that non-duality. (UtAjP 27)

Vṛtti: Relying upon non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*), and because within this entire universe—which consists of the manifestation of differentiation—there is the manifestness of blue, pleasure, and so forth, which appear externally through the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) precisely by virtue of their remaining undiminished within [consciousness];
and furthermore, by relying on non-difference, the manifestation of the inert (*jaḍa*) is possible, whereas otherwise it would not be manifested;
for that reason, in the venerable *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, the universe is said to have non-dual consciousness as its very nature. May there be auspiciousness! (*śivam*).
"In the year [measured by] the moon, the oceans, the eight, and the moon (1841) of the Śaka era, Hara composed this commentary on the *Pramātṛsiddhi* written by the teacher Utpaladeva.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi*, composed by the venerable Mahāmāheśvara teacher Utpaladeva.
By the command of the illustrious Lord Pratāpa, this work has been prepared by Madhusūdana Kaula for the delight of the virtuous and is now published.
